vignette:
For seventy-two years, Harold had lived a life of quiet precision. As a software engineer, he had spent decades solving problems with logic, building systems that were elegant and predictable. Then, six months ago, on a business trip to a country he'd only ever seen on a map, that world ended. He had been taken from his hotel room by men who accused him of industrial espionage, a charge so absurd it took him days to understand it wasn't a mistake. For three weeks, they kept him in a concrete room. They asked questions he couldn't answer, and when he couldn't, they hurt him in ways that made him feel his body was no longer his own. He had told them everything he knew, which was nothing, and then he had told them things he made up, just to make the pain stop. That was the worst part. He had always believed he was a man of integrity, someone who would never break. Now, he was certain he had acted in ways that go against who he fundamentally is. He had lost his faith in people, in life, in the very idea of order. He felt isolated and set apart from everyone, even his own colleagues, who had no idea what he had been through.

Back in his own apartment, the threat didn't end. It had followed him home. He studied every face on the street, every shift in body language, trying to detect the next threat before it materialized. He had come to believe that danger was everywhere, that anyone could be a predator. This constant scanning meant he was always on edge, and it fed a deeper, more corrosive belief: that he was fundamentally different now, a contaminated person who could never be understood. Because he felt so isolated and set apart, he began to rely on rigid, private rules to manage his terror. He started to monitor his own thoughts constantly, terrified that he was finally going crazy. He believed that if he didn't keep a tight grip on his mind, he would unravel completely. He also tried desperately not to think about the trauma, but the harder he suppressed the memories, the more they seemed to intrude.

The threat felt most acute at home. He checked the locks on his doors and windows repeatedly, sometimes four or five times before he could sit down. He had difficulty falling asleep because he needed to stay alert, listening for footsteps in the hall. This hypervigilance, in turn, made him feel even more isolated. It was impossible to connect with anyone when he was constantly assessing them as a potential danger. He avoided being alone in a room or a building, a strategy that was both a solution and a source of shame. He would leave his apartment just to stand in the lobby, where other people were, even though he couldn't bear to speak to them. This avoidance only deepened his conviction that he was broken, that he was the only one living in this state of siege. The more he monitored his thoughts and suppressed them, the more he felt he had lost his faith in everything-a self-reinforcing loop where his very attempts to cope proved to him that he was, indeed, going mad.

The cycle tightened. His constant threat scanning made him feel more isolated. His isolation drove him to more extreme maladaptive strategies, like his thought monitoring. And those strategies-the constant checking, the suppression, the avoidance of solitude-only proved to him that he was a fundamentally changed and lost person. He had stopped going to the office, working remotely from a café where he could keep his back to the wall. His productivity had plummeted. His boss had called, concerned. Harold couldn't explain. What finally brought him to seek help was a simple, terrifying realization: he was losing the only thing he had left-his mind. He was most afraid that a therapist would confirm what he already suspected: that he was irreparably damaged, and that the man he used to be was gone forever.
